Without Genghis Khan, the modern world would not be possible. 30-70 million people died as a direct result of his conquests, he decimated entire towns, cities and cultures, and untold amounts of cumulative knowledge has been lost (e.g. siege of Baghdad). The Middle East suffered a blow from which it never truly recovered and he managed to conquer China in its entirety and decimate numerous united European forces.

But Genghis Khan was religiously tolerant. His religion, Shamanism, revolved around the natural landscape of Mongolia and the Gobi desert. He understood that people from different areas wouldn't have the same religion, and he didn't expect them to. He was perfectly okay with everyone in his rule to practice their own religion. Along with religious tolerance, the Mongols created an extremely widespread and fast postal system, sending letters traveling at the speed of horseback. The postal system covered the span of the Mongol empire and brought people together in a way never before seen, especially in Asia. Genghis Khan also allowed ideas to spread; by bringing people together under one rule, one empire and one language, it was very easy for ideas to spread and people to learn and create new technologies or ideas. It was more convenient than ever for people to share ideas and learn. The Mongol empire was also safe -- Genghis Khan created his own set of laws, called the Yassa, which were very strictlye enforced. It was said that a woman could walk the span of the Mongol empire with a pot of gold on her head without fear of being raped or mugged. Lastly but most importantly, Genghis Khan was pretty much the driving force in the European era of enlightenment (renaissance era). By revitalising the silk road, Genghis Khan jump-started international trade and innovation, helped out by the aforementioned idea-sharing. This massive age of enlightenment gave us new technologies, medicines and laws that we have been able to modify and evolve along with our society, and we very much rely on today.

So was all of this worth killing 10% of the world's population? It's easy to say yes, because we didn't know any of these people. In the end it's impossible to say for sure -- we're not the ones who paid the bill. But do you think this is all worth it for the cost of those tens of millions of lives?

What You See Is What You Get.

This was a big issue in the 80s and 90s, when word processors used special codes and the like to show where a document had to be, for instance, underlined, or italicized. Most of the earliest word processors (e.g. WordStar) were just based on the default monospace terminal font when they were on the computer screen. Often this was because they were written for computers that had limited (or no) graphics capabilities - literally text-only terminals with some text characters that vaguely resembled things you could build primitive user interfaces with.

WYSIWIG was a big breakthrough at the time, because for once you could actually see what you were trying to make as you were making it, and because it had a good bit more complexity, since you were either writing for a GUI (which was relatively new at the time, and often had other bits of programming difficulty going with it, e.g. participating in cooperative multitasking), or you were writing your own code which meant you often had to start from scratch, and even if you didn't, the process of writing code to render a document from scratch is no easy feat. There's a reason why there was a great deal of code written into most GUIs (including Windows, Mac OS and X) to handle fonts, and even simple rich text editor widgets, 'cuz it's damned tough even with the tools a modern UI API provides.
